Nympha
NIM-fuh
proper noun (figure)
Greek Nympha (feminine) or Nymphas (masculine); the manuscripts differ on the gender. Related to nymphē ("bride, young woman"). A believer in Laodicea (or nearby) in whose house a church met (Col 4:15).

📖 Biblical Definition

Nympha was a believer in the region of Laodicea in whose house a church gathered, named in the closing greetings of Paul's letter to the Colossians: "Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house" (Col 4:15). The Greek manuscripts differ on whether the name is feminine (Nympha) or masculine (Nymphas), and correspondingly on whether the house is "her house" or "his house" — a textual question that does not affect the doctrine but reflects the early uncertainty; many modern texts read the feminine, "Nympha... her house." Whether man or woman, Nympha holds the significant distinction of being one of several New-Testament believers in whose homes the early church met: the church in the house of Priscilla and Aquila (Rom 16:5; 1 Cor 16:19), the church in the house of Philemon (Philem 2), and the church in the house of Nympha (Col 4:15). These "house churches" were the ordinary form of Christian assembly in the apostolic age, before the church had buildings of its own: believers gathered in the homes of members able to host them, for the reading of Scripture, prayer, the Lord's Supper, and fellowship. To open one's home to the church was a real and costly service — it meant hospitality, expense, risk in times of persecution, and the disruption of one's household for the sake of the gathered saints. Nympha did this, and is named forever for it. If, as many hold, Nympha was a woman, she joins Priscilla, Lydia, Phoebe, and others among the women whose homes, resources, and labor advanced the early church — honored not by holding the teaching office (which Scripture reserves to qualified men) but by the indispensable ministries of hospitality, support, and service that the gospel opens to all the saints. The naming of Nympha reminds the church of the foundational ministry of Christian hospitality — the opening of homes for the gathering and good of God's people.

NYMPHA, proper noun. Greek Nympha (feminine) or Nymphas (masculine); the manuscripts differ.

A believer in the region of Laodicea in whose house a church gathered (Col 4:15).

One of several NT house-church hosts: Priscilla and Aquila (Rom 16:5), Philemon (Philem 2), Nympha (Col 4:15).

House churches were the ordinary apostolic-age assembly, before the church had its own buildings.

The model of Christian hospitality: opening the home for the gathering and good of God's people.

📖 Key Scripture

Colossians 4:15 — "Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house."

Romans 16:5 — "Likewise greet the church that is in their house. Salute my well-beloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ."

Romans 12:13 — "Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality."

1 Peter 4:9 — "Use hospitality one to another without grudging."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Nympha is corrupted when the house-church and the ministry of hospitality are forgotten, when the textual question of the name's gender is made a battleground for agendas the text does not serve, or when the indispensable supporting ministries of the saints are undervalued beside the teaching office.

expand to see more

Hospitality-forgotten. The house churches of the apostolic age — in the homes of Priscilla and Aquila, Philemon, and Nympha — depended on believers willing to open their homes for the gathering of the saints. This was costly hospitality: expense, disruption, and in times of persecution real danger. Scripture commands hospitality of all believers (Rom 12:13; 1 Pet 4:9; Heb 13:2), and the named house-church hosts model it at the foundation of the church's life. A church culture that has professionalized and outsourced hospitality, and that no longer opens homes for the good of God's people, has lost something the early church held precious. Nympha opened a home; the church should learn the grace again.

Gender-debate over-reading. The textual question of whether the name is Nympha (feminine) or Nymphas (masculine) has been pressed into modern debates over women's ministry, with some eager to read "a woman leading a house church" as warrant for women in the teaching/governing office. The text will not bear the weight: hosting a church in one's home is the ministry of hospitality, not the holding of the teaching office, which Scripture reserves to qualified men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:1-7). If Nympha was a woman, she joins the honored company of women whose homes, resources, and labor served the church — a ministry the dictionary gladly honors, distinct from the eldership the New Testament orders otherwise. The dictionary holds the complementarian position; the house of Nympha neither establishes nor overturns it, because hosting a gathering is not the same as holding the office.
